Neonatal Black-bellied pangolins (Phataginus tetradactyla) are born with a total length averaging approximately 32.5 centimeters [Lb = approximately 32.5 centimeters], a size drawn from a documented range of 30 to 35 centimeters across litters. This modest initial dimension contrasts sharply with the species' ultimate adult length, as fully grown individuals can attain a maximum total body length of 120 centimeters [Li = 120 centimeters], a measurement that includes the long prehensile tail characteristic of arboreal pangolins. The relatively small size at birth is accompanied by a low neonatal wet weight; newborns typically emerge weighing around 125 grams [Wwb = around 125 grams], drawn from a documented range of 100 to 150 grams across litters. This substantial growth trajectory from a 32.5-centimeter neonate to a 120-centimeter adult reflects a period of rapid somatic development facilitated by intensive maternal care during the early suckling phase.

Reproduction in Phataginus tetradactyla is governed by a combination of gestation length and postpartum fertility. Females experience a gestation period of approximately 140 days [tg = approximately 140 days], after which a single offspring is typically delivered. Remarkably, females are capable of becoming pregnant again almost immediately following parturition, producing a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and can raise up to approximately 2 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 litters per year]. The combined duration of gestation and subsequent postpartum pregnancy allows for a potentially high annual fecundity, although this is tempered by the prolonged period of offspring dependence. The ability to conceive shortly after birth, while energetically demanding, is a strategy observed in several pangolin species and appears to maximize lifetime reproductive output in environments where food resources are seasonally abundant.

Sexual maturity in the Black-bellied pangolin is attained relatively slowly compared to its rapid postpartum reproductive capacity. Field estimates suggest that individuals reach puberty at approximately two years since birth [tp = approximately two years since birth], a timeline that allows for substantial somatic growth before the energetically costly demands of reproduction begin. This age at maturity corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of roughly 1,100 grams [Wwp = roughly 1,100 grams], which represents the minimum adult body mass reported for the species and marks the threshold at which individuals are considered reproductively viable. The delay in reaching this mass until roughly 730 days old is thought to reflect the time required to develop the robust musculoskeletal system necessary for arboreal foraging and predator avoidance in the dense forest canopy.

The transition to nutritional independence is a gradual process in Phataginus tetradactyla. Offspring begin to consume solid food at a few weeks of age but continue to nurse from the mother for an extended period. Field observations indicate that the typical age at weaning is approximately 91.5 days [tx = approximately 91.5 days], a duration that corresponds to roughly three months after birth. This weaning age, equivalent to about 91 days, coincides with the point at which the young pangolin has achieved sufficient body size and foraging competence to accompany the mother on feeding excursions. The protracted lactation period, lasting just over a quarter of a year, ensures that the juvenile receives both immunological protection and nutritional support during the vulnerable early months of life, after which the mother may become pregnant again with the next offspring.

Longevity data for the Black-bellied pangolin remain sparse, but estimates derived from the closely related Phataginus tricuspis, based on the oldest individual documented in captivity, suggest a potential maximum lifespan of approximately ten years [am = approximately ten years]. This comparatively short life span, equivalent to roughly 3,650 days [am = roughly 3,650 days], is consistent with the life-history strategy of a relatively small mammal that invests heavily in early reproduction. The ultimate wet weight attained by healthy adult Phataginus tetradactyla has been recorded at approximately 3,600 grams [Wwi = approximately 3,600 grams], a metric that distinguishes this species as the largest of the African tree pangolins. This robust adult body mass, achieved through a combination of efficient foraging on ants and termites and a low basal metabolic rate, supports the species' fully arboreal lifestyle and its ability to sustain the energetic demands of gestation and lactation.
